title: A/B Testing
summary: A/B = one change, one metric — not random experiments

sections.heading: Orientation
sections.subtitle: Orientation
sections.contentMarkdown:
- What will you understand? An A/B Test means changing one thing and measuring one result — not multiple random experiments at the same time.
- Why now? After learning about interpretation errors, you need a method to ensure that the change is the cause of the result — not a coincidence or noise in the data.
- What after the lesson? You will design a simple A/B test: what you are comparing, what the one variable is, what the metric is, and the duration of observation before making a decision.

sections.heading: Tension
sections.subtitle: A Familiar Situation
sections.contentMarkdown:
- You changed the headline, price, and image in the same week — sales increased. You might say, "So everything worked!"
- This is not an A/B test — this is chaos. Too many variables = no lesson can be learned from the experiment.
- AI (artificial intelligence) helps you formulate a hypothesis and interpret the result — but you must define one variable and one metric before you start.

sections.heading: Core Idea
sections.subtitle: A vs B — One Variable — Metric Before Starting
sections.contentMarkdown:
- A/B = Version A (as is) versus Version B (only one change). Everything else is constant.
- Define the metric before starting: Conversion, Clicks, Revenue — not "let's see what happens."
- Beginner's warning: Small sample = unreliable result. 2–4 weeks of observation is better than just 3 days.
- AI helps you formulate the hypothesis and interpretation — but don’t overstate: don’t say "we proved 100%" from just 20 visitors.

sections.subtitle: Terms for Testing

sections.heading: Mission
sections.subtitle: Design a Simple A/B Test
sections.contentMarkdown:
Introduction: This is a design task — not a mandatory operation. Write an A/B test: what you are comparing, what the variable is, the metric, and the duration of observation. AI may suggest wording — you choose the final version. Delivery: 1. What you are comparing (A vs B — brief description)
2. The one variable that changed
3. The metric — defined before starting
4. Duration of observation + where to measure
5. Potential decision if B succeeds — and if it fails Mission template: ```
A vs B:
A: [current version]
B: [the only change] The one variable:
[What changed — headline / price / CTA…] The metric:
[Metric — example: Conversion %] Observation:
[Duration — example: two weeks] + [Where — page / email…] Decision if B succeeds:
[Then I will…] Decision if B fails:
[Then I will…]
``` Evaluation criteria: | Dimension | Weight | Criteria |
|-------|-------|---------|
| Variable + Metric | 60% | One variable + metric defined before starting |
| Observation + Decision | 40% | Realistic duration + potential decision for success and failure |
